answer: The indexed Xeljanz prescribing information (dated November 10, 2026) warns that patients with rheumatoid arthritis aged 50 and older with at least one cardiovascular risk factor had higher rates of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and all-cause mortality compared to those treated with TNF blockers. According to the November 10, 2026 prescribing information, RA Safety Study 1 failed to meet its non-inferiority criterion for MACE because the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval exceeded 1.8 when comparing combined tofacitinib doses to TNF blockers. The indexed prescribing information (dated November 10, 2026) lists MACE incidence rates per 100 patient-years in RA Safety Study 1 as 1.11 for tofacitinib 10 mg twice daily, 0.91 for 5 mg twice daily, and 0.79 for TNF blockers. In a September 1, 2021 safety communication, the FDA concluded from a randomized clinical trial in patients with rheumatoid arthritis that tofacitinib is associated with an increased risk of serious heart-related events compared to TNF blockers. The FDA stated on September 1, 2021, that it required updated warnings regarding major adverse cardiovascular events across Janus kinase inhibitors following the trial evaluation. In the randomized, open-label ORAL Surveillance trial of rheumatoid arthritis patients aged 50 and older with cardiovascular risk factors, combined tofacitinib doses yielded higher risks of MACE compared to a TNF inhibitor and failed noninferiority criteria. In the observational STAR-RA cohort study of routine care rheumatoid arthritis patients, researchers did not observe an increased risk of cardiovascular outcomes with tofacitinib versus TNF inhibitors, though an increased risk was non-significantly observed in patients with baseline cardiovascular risk factors. Both the randomized ORAL Surveillance study and the indexed label (dated November 10, 2026) report that tofacitinib missed non-inferiority benchmarks for MACE versus TNF blockers in older RA patients with cardiovascular risk factors.
